items.title: The Windrush passengers were British subjects, not foreign immigrants
items.claim: On 22 June 1948 the HMT Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury with 492 passengers from the Caribbean. Their legal status?

options.text: They required visas and work permits
They were British subjects with full right of entry — the British Nationality Act 1948 confirmed Commonwealth citizens' status, passed weeks after Windrush
They were refugees with temporary leave
They were on military service tickets only

items.reveal:
The British Nationality Act 1948 (royal assent 30 July 1948) defined 'Citizens of the United Kingdom and Colonies' alongside Commonwealth citizenship. Caribbean people were British subjects; the journey required no permit.

The 1971 Immigration Act removed automatic right of abode for most Commonwealth citizens. People who had arrived as children before 1973 should have had right to remain, but the Home Office destroyed landing card records in 2010 — leading to the Windrush scandal of 2018, when long-resident citizens were detained, deported or denied healthcare.

The Windrush brought around 1,000 passengers total, including Jamaicans returning from RAF service.
items.why: Right of abode in Britain has been redefined repeatedly. The 1948-1973 period when Commonwealth citizens had unrestricted entry is bracketed by very different regimes — and the 2018 scandal shows what happens when administrative memory fails.

items.title: One Soviet officer's veto prevented nuclear war in 1962
items.claim: On 27 October 1962, a Soviet submarine (B-59) near Cuba was being depth-charged by the US Navy. The captain ordered a nuclear torpedo prepared for launch. Why didn't it fire?

options.text: Launch required the unanimous consent of three officers; Second Captain Vasily Arkhipov refused
Kennedy's blockade orders explicitly forbade depth-charging Soviet submarines
The submarine surfaced before the launch could be authorised

items.reveal_title: The man who saved the world
items.reveal:
B-59 had been submerged for days, the air was foul, the crew thought war had begun. Captain Valentin Savitsky and political officer Ivan Maslennikov voted to fire. Arkhipov, brigade chief of staff and equal in rank, refused.

Under Soviet protocol, all three had to agree. Arkhipov persuaded Savitsky to surface and await orders. The story only emerged publicly in 2002 at a conference marking the crisis's 40th anniversary; Thomas Blanton of the National Security Archive said 'a guy called Vasily Arkhipov saved the world.'
items.why: Macro-historical narratives about MAD (mutually assured destruction) keeping the peace miss that systems are only as safe as the individuals inside them. Nuclear war was a vote away.

items.title: Charles I lost the Civil War partly because he was a poor commander
items.claim: What contributed to Charles I's defeat (1642-1646) beyond political 'tyranny'?

options.text: Parliamentary forces always vastly outnumbered the king's

Parliament held London (wealth, manpower), the navy, and after 1645 the New Model Army; Charles repeatedly failed to coordinate his commanders and missed strategic opportunities like marching on London after Edgehill
The Scots refused to fight on either side
Charles was killed in battle at Naseby

items.reveal_title: The man, not just the cause
items.reveal:
After the indecisive Edgehill (October 1642), Charles failed to march on London while it was undefended. The Solemn League and Covenant (1643) brought Scottish forces in on Parliament's side. The New Model Army (formed 1645) under Fairfax and Cromwell was the first national professional army.

Charles surrendered to the Scots in 1646; they handed him to Parliament. His attempts to negotiate while plotting a second war (the 'Engagement' with the Scots, 1647) destroyed any remaining trust and led to his trial.
items.why: Wars are won by armies, logistics and leadership — not just by who has the better political argument. Charles's strategic failures are often glossed over in the rush to debate 'tyranny vs liberty'.
